result.note: Tests the January 2026 Economic Survey's proposals on ultra-processed foods and digital addiction; these are Survey recommendations, not enacted policy.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about the Economic Survey presented in January 2026 and its treatment of ultra-processed foods (UPFs):
items: It suggested moving UPFs to the highest GST slab along with a surcharge.
It proposed replacing front-of-pack warning labels with star-based health ratings.
It noted that obesity has doubled alongside a 150% jump in UPF consumption over 15 years.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: Statement 2 is wrong. The Survey proposed the reverse, replacing vague ratings with clear front-of-pack warning labels. Its toolkit also included banning UPF marketing during daytime and evening hours across media.
questions.source: The Survey notes that obesity has doubled alongside a 150% jump in UPF consumption over 15 years and significantly increasing healthcare costs and decreasing productivity.

questions.prompt: The Economic Survey presented in January 2026 flagged compulsive digital use as a productivity threat. Consider the following statements about its suggestions:
items: It floated age-based access limits for social media and gambling apps.
It suggested basic phones for children to curb early addiction.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explain: Both suggestions appear in the Survey, along with a proposed digital wellness curriculum in schools. It linked digital over-consumption to anxiety and sleep deprivation and warned that this could blunt India's demographic dividend.
questions.source: It floats age-based access limits for social media and gambling apps, proposes a “digital wellness curriculum” in schools, and even suggests basic phones for children to curb early addiction.
